name: Boeing 737-800
numberBuilt: 7,124 737 Next Generation aircraft of all models
summary: The 737-800 is the most popular member of Boeing's 737 Next Generation family, a single-aisle jet built for flights of a few hours. It has been the backbone of Australian domestic flying for over 20 years, so it is one of the aeroplanes you are most likely to fly on between Melbourne and Sydney, Brisbane or Perth.
funFacts: More than 7,000 737 Next Generation jets were built, and the 737-800 is by far the most common version.
The RAAF's P-8A Poseidon submarine-hunting aircraft is a military version of the 737-800, packed with sensors instead of passenger seats.
The 737 sits so low to the ground that its engines have slightly flattened bottoms so they do not scrape the runway.
Boeing stopped building passenger 737-800s in 2020, but military versions are still being made.
spotterTips: Look for two engines with flattened lower lips tucked close under the wings, and tall upturned winglets on most aircraft. It is longer than the A320 and its nose is more pointed, with a cockpit window line that dips at the corners.

melbourne.where: Seen all day at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on domestic and short international flights. You can also watch them from the Melbourne Airport viewing areas off Sharps Road.

name: Boeing 737 MAX 8
numberBuilt: 2,483 737 MAX aircraft of all models (by September 2026)
summary: The 737 MAX 8 is the newest version of the Boeing 737, with bigger, more efficient engines and redesigned wingtips. It carries about the same number of people as the 737-800 but uses less fuel and can fly further.
funFacts: The 737 MAX was grounded around the world for about 20 months from March 2019 while Boeing fixed a problem with its flight control software.
Its LEAP-1B engines are so large that Boeing had to make the nose landing gear taller and move the engines further forward on the wing.
The MAX has split-tip winglets that point both up and down, which help it use less fuel.
More than 4,800 737 MAX jets were still waiting to be built and delivered in late 2026.
spotterTips: The easiest clues are the split winglets that point both up and down, and the zig-zag (sawtooth) edges at the back of the engine covers. The engines are rounder and sit further forward than on a 737-800.

melbourne.where: Regularly flies in and out of Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on domestic and short international routes.

name: Airbus A320
engines: 2 × CFM International CFM56-5B or IAE V2500 turbofans
summary: The A320 is a single-aisle airliner and the main member of the A320 family, the best-selling airliner family in the world. It was the first airliner to use digital fly-by-wire controls, meaning the pilots' inputs go to computers that then move the control surfaces.
funFacts: Instead of a big control wheel, A320 pilots fly with a small sidestick beside their seat, a bit like a gaming joystick.
The A320 family overtook the Boeing 737 as the best-selling airliner family in 2019.
Around 12,900 A320 family jets have been built, which works out to more than one new jet rolling out every day for decades.
Newer A320s have upturned wingtips called sharklets, while older ones have small fences that point both up and down.
spotterTips: Compared with a 737, the A320 has a rounder, blunter nose, a cockpit window line that is straight across, and round engines hanging lower below the wing. Older ones have small triangular wingtip fences, newer ones have tall curved sharklets.

melbourne.where: Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) is the home base of Jetstar, so A320s are everywhere there. You may also see them at Avalon Airport.

name: Airbus A321neo and A321XLR
nickname: XLR (for the extra long range version)
specsVariant: A321neo (97 t version); the A321XLR can fly up to about 8,700 km
engines: 2 × CFM LEAP-1A or Pratt & Whitney PW1100G geared turbofans
summary: The A321neo is the longest member of the A320 family, fitted with new fuel-saving engines (neo stands for new engine option). The A321XLR version carries extra fuel so a single-aisle jet can fly routes that once needed a big wide-body, such as Australia to parts of Asia.
funFacts: The A321XLR first flew on 15 June 2022 from Hamburg, Germany.
The XLR has an extra fuel tank built into the rear of its belly, letting it fly about 4,700 nautical miles (about 8,700 km).
The A321neo entered service on 31 May 2017 with Virgin America in the United States.
Qantas chose the A321XLR to replace its Boeing 737-800s on many routes.
spotterTips: It looks like a stretched A320 with big round engines and sharklet wingtips. Count the doors: the A321 has extra exits over or near the wing, and its body looks noticeably long and thin.

melbourne.where: Common at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on domestic and trans-Tasman flights.

name: Airbus A330
engines: 2 × General Electric CF6, Pratt & Whitney PW4000 or Rolls-Royce Trent 700 turbofans
summary: The A330 is a twin-engine wide-body jet with two aisles, used for flights across Australia and to Asia and the Pacific. It shares its wing with the four-engine A340 and its cockpit with the A320, which made it easy for airlines to train pilots on several Airbus types.
funFacts: The RAAF's KC-30A air-to-air refuelling tankers are military versions of the A330-200.
The A330 and the four-engine A340 were developed together and use the same wing.
Customers could choose from three different engine makers for the original A330.
More than 1,600 A330s have been built since it first flew in 1992.
spotterTips: Look for a big twin-engine jet with two aisles' worth of fuselage, small upturned winglets and a rounded Airbus nose. Its main landing gear has four wheels on each leg, which helps tell it apart from the six-wheel 777.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on flights to Perth and Asia. RAAF KC-30A tankers based on the A330 often appear at the Avalon Airshow.

name: Airbus A330neo
summary: The A330neo is an updated A330 with new Rolls-Royce engines and a longer wing, so it burns less fuel and can fly further. It entered service in December 2018 with TAP Air Portugal.
funFacts: The Trent 7000 is the only engine available for the A330neo, so every one is powered by Rolls-Royce.
Its wingspan grew to 64 m thanks to new curved sharklet wingtips, about 3.7 m wider than the original A330.
There are two models, the A330-800 and the larger A330-900, and the -900 is much more popular.
neo stands for new engine option.
spotterTips: It looks like an A330 but with large, curved sharklet wingtips instead of small winglets, and bigger engines with a different shape. Many also have the cockpit windows outlined in black, like the A350.

melbourne.where: Occasionally seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on flights from Asia and the Pacific.

name: Boeing 787 Dreamliner
engines: 2 × General Electric GEnx-1B or Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 turbofans
summary: The 787 Dreamliner was the first airliner with most of its body and wings made from carbon fibre composite instead of aluminium. That makes it light and efficient enough to fly very long routes, such as non-stop from Australia to Europe.
funFacts: On 25 March 2018 a Qantas 787-9 flew the first scheduled non-stop flight from Australia to the UK, from Perth to London in about 17 hours.
Instead of window shades, the 787 has electronic windows that passengers dim with a button.
Its wings bend upwards a lot in flight, which is normal and makes the wingtips look like they are curving towards the sky.
The back edges of the engine covers have zig-zag chevrons that help make the engines quieter.
spotterTips: Look for long, very flexible wings that curve up at the tips with no winglets (raked wingtips), zig-zag edges on the engine covers, and a smooth, rounded nose with four cockpit windows.

melbourne.where: A daily sight at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on long-haul flights to North America, Asia, the Middle East and New Zealand.
melbourne.operators: Qantas, Air New Zealand, United Airlines, plus many visiting airlines

name: Airbus A350
summary: The A350 is Airbus's newest long-range wide-body jet, built largely from carbon fibre composites like the Boeing 787. It is quiet, efficient and can fly some of the longest routes in the world.
funFacts: In July 2026 an A350-1000ULR test aircraft built for Qantas flew non-stop from Toulouse in France to Melbourne in about 19 hours and 12 minutes.
Qantas ordered 12 A350-1000s for Project Sunrise, its plan for non-stop flights from Sydney to London and New York.
The black mask painted around the cockpit windows is a design feature that makes it look a bit like a raccoon.
Every A350 is powered by Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines, the only engine offered for it.
spotterTips: The dark mask around the cockpit windows is the giveaway. It also has wingtips that curve smoothly upwards and two large engines with no zig-zag edges.

melbourne.where: Seen daily at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on flights to Asia and the Middle East.
melbourne.operators: Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Qatar Airways and other international airlines

name: Airbus A380
engines: 4 × Rolls-Royce Trent 900 or Engine Alliance GP7200 turbofans
summary: The A380 is the largest passenger airliner ever built, with two full decks running the whole length of the aeroplane. It is so big that airports had to build special gates with extra air bridges to load both decks.
funFacts: Its wings are about 79.75 m from tip to tip and cover 845 square metres, bigger than three tennis courts.
Emirates is by far the biggest A380 operator, with more than 100 of them.
Only 251 A380s were delivered to airlines before production ended.
The tail is 24 m tall, about the height of an eight-storey building.
spotterTips: Two full rows of windows from nose to tail, four engines and a huge, thick wing make it unmistakable. The nose has a rounded, bulbous shape with the cockpit tucked between the two decks.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on long-haul flights, especially to Dubai. Its size makes it easy to spot even from a distance.

name: Boeing 777
summary: The 777 is the world's largest twin-engine airliner family in service and one of the most successful long-haul jets ever. The 777-300ER can carry nearly as many people as a 747 with only two engines.
funFacts: The GE90-115B engines on the 777-300ER are among the most powerful jet engines ever built, each producing about 115,000 pounds of thrust.
The 777 was the first Boeing airliner designed entirely on computers.
Each main landing gear leg has six wheels, so a 777 lands on twelve main wheels plus two at the nose.
The 777 entered service with United Airlines on 7 June 1995.
spotterTips: Look for two enormous engines, a long body and six-wheel main landing gear. The tail cone at the back ends in a sharp, flat blade shape instead of a rounded point.

melbourne.where: Seen daily at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on long-haul flights to the Middle East, Asia and beyond.
melbourne.operators: Emirates, Qatar Airways and other international airlines

name: Boeing 747
nickname: Jumbo Jet, Queen of the Skies
summary: The 747 was the original Jumbo Jet, the first wide-body airliner, and it made long-distance flying affordable for millions of people. Production ended in 2023 after more than 50 years, and today most 747s still flying carry cargo.
funFacts: In 1991 an El Al 747 carried 1,087 passengers in a single flight during Operation Solomon, an airlift from Ethiopia to Israel.
The famous hump was designed so the nose could swing open for loading cargo, with the cockpit moved up out of the way.
The 747 was the first airliner to use an inertial navigation system, so it did not need a navigator in the cockpit.
Its maximum takeoff weight grew from about 333 tonnes on the 747-100 to about 440 tonnes on the 747-8.
spotterTips: The hump at the front of the upper deck is the giveaway, plus four engines under the wings. The 747-400 and 747-8 also have upturned or raked wingtips.

melbourne.where: Mostly seen as cargo freighters at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine), often at night or early morning. Qantas retired its last passenger 747 in 2020.

name: Boeing 777X
summary: The 777X is the next generation of the Boeing 777, with new carbon fibre wings and the GE9X, the largest jet engine ever built. The 777-9 will be the longest airliner ever, and it is due to start carrying passengers in 2027.
funFacts: Its wingtips fold upwards on the ground so it can fit into the same airport gates as a normal 777.
At 76.73 m long, the 777-9 is longer than both the 747-8 and the A380.
The 777-9 first flew on 25 January 2020, but certification delays have pushed its first deliveries back several years.
The fan at the front of each GE9X engine is about 3.4 m across, almost as wide as the body of a Boeing 737.
spotterTips: Look for the hinge line near each wingtip where the folding tips sit, and huge engines on a very long body. It has raked, pointed wingtips with no winglets.

name: COMAC C919
summary: The C919 is China's first large home-grown jet airliner, designed to compete with the Airbus A320 and Boeing 737. It carried its first paying passengers on 28 May 2023 with China Eastern Airlines.
funFacts: Although it is Chinese-designed, its LEAP-1C engines come from CFM International, a joint company of GE (United States) and Safran (France).
It is almost exactly the same size as an A320, with a wingspan of 35.8 m.
COMAC has planned longer and shorter versions as well as an extended-range model.
spotterTips: It looks very similar to an A320, with round engines under the wings and upturned winglets. The COMAC name and Chinese airline colours are the best clues.

name: Airbus A220
summary: The A220 was designed in Canada by Bombardier as the CSeries and became an Airbus in 2018. It is a modern, quiet jet sized between regional planes and the A320, and QantasLink flies it from Melbourne.
funFacts: QantasLink began A220 passenger flights on 1 March 2024, flying from Melbourne to Canberra and Brisbane.
QantasLink's first A220 was painted in an Aboriginal art livery called Minyma Kutjara Tjukurpa.
Its geared turbofan engines have a gearbox so the big fan can spin slower than the engine core, which saves fuel and reduces noise.
The economy cabin has a 2-3 layout, so only one side has a middle seat.
spotterTips: Look for a slim jet with very large engines for its size, big rectangular-ish windows and a small curved winglet. The nose is short and rounded.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on QantasLink domestic flights.

name: Embraer E190
summary: The E190 is a Brazilian regional jet from the E-Jet family, built for routes that are too busy for a turboprop but too small for a 737 or A320. Australia's Alliance Airlines is the world's largest E190 operator.
funFacts: Alliance Airlines operates 64 E190s, more than any other airline in the world.
E-Jets have a double-bubble shaped body with a 2-2 seat layout, so there are no middle seats.
Embraer is based in Brazil and is the third-largest maker of airliners after Airbus and Boeing.
The newer E190-E2 version has bigger geared turbofan engines and a longer wing.
spotterTips: Look for a small twin jet with engines under the wings, a long slender nose and a low-slung body. It is shorter than a 737 and its tail fin is tall and slightly swept.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on regional and charter flights, sometimes flying on behalf of the major airlines.

name: Fokker 100
summary: The Fokker 100 is a Dutch-built regional jet with its two engines mounted at the back and a T-shaped tail. Fokker stopped making aircraft in the 1990s, but Australia became one of the last strongholds of the type, flying workers to mines in remote areas.
funFacts: Production ended in 1997 after Fokker went bankrupt, so every Fokker 100 flying today is at least 28 years old.
Qantas donated retired Fokker 100s to the Historical Aircraft Restoration Society museum at Parkes in New South Wales.
Australian operators used the type heavily for fly-in fly-out mining flights.
spotterTips: Two engines mounted on the rear fuselage beside a tall T-tail, with a clean wing that has no engines under it. It looks a bit like a smaller, sleeker DC-9.

melbourne.where: Occasionally seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on charter flights.

name: De Havilland Canada Dash 8 Q400
summary: The Q400 is the largest and fastest member of the Dash 8 family of propeller-driven regional airliners. It links smaller cities to the big airports and is almost as quick as a jet on short routes.
funFacts: The Q stands for quiet, because these aircraft have a system that reduces noise and vibration in the cabin.
With a high-speed cruise of up to about 667 km/h, the Q400 is one of the fastest turboprop airliners flying.
Production of the Dash 8 has been paused since 2022 while De Havilland Canada plans a new factory.
spotterTips: A high wing with two big engines, each spinning a six-blade propeller, and a T-tail. The main landing gear folds into the engine pods and the body is long and slim.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on regional flights to other cities in Victoria, New South Wales and Tasmania.

name: Saab 340
summary: The Saab 340 is a small Swedish turboprop airliner with 34 seats, built for short regional hops. In Australia it is the workhorse of Rex (Regional Express), linking country towns with the capital cities.
funFacts: It was designed by Saab, the Swedish company that also builds the Gripen fighter jet.
The project started as a partnership with Fairchild in the United States, which is why early ones were called the SF340.
Rex in Australia has been one of the biggest Saab 340 operators in the world.
spotterTips: A small, low-wing turboprop with two engines and four-blade propellers, a pointed nose and a tall, swept tail fin.

melbourne.where: Seen at Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on regional flights to country towns in Victoria, New South Wales, Tasmania and King Island.

name: ATR 72
summary: The ATR 72 is a twin turboprop airliner built by a French and Italian partnership. It is one of the most popular regional aircraft in the world because it is cheap to run on short routes.
funFacts: ATR is a joint company owned by Airbus and the Italian firm Leonardo.
Passengers usually board through a door at the back, while cargo goes in a door at the front.
It first entered service with Finnair in 1989.
The latest ATR 72-600 can carry up to 72 passengers, which is where the name comes from.
spotterTips: A high wing mounted on top of the body, two engines with six-blade propellers, a T-tail, and main landing gear that folds into bulges on the sides of the body rather than into the engines.

name: De Havilland Canada Twin Otter
manufacturer: De Havilland Canada (also built by Viking Air)
role: Short takeoff and landing (STOL) utility aircraft
summary: The Twin Otter is a rugged small turboprop that can take off and land on very short, rough strips, snow or water. It is used everywhere from Antarctic research bases to tropical island hops.
funFacts: It can be fitted with wheels, skis or floats, so it can operate from runways, snow and ice, or lakes and the sea.
Production stopped in 1988 but was restarted by Viking Air, and the 1,000th Twin Otter was delivered in 2026.
Its fixed landing gear never retracts, which keeps it simple and tough for rough strips.
spotterTips: A boxy body, a high straight wing braced by struts, two engines on the wing and fixed landing gear with a nose wheel. It looks a bit like a flying minibus.

name: Boeing 777 Freighter
engines: 2 × General Electric GE90-110B or GE90-115B turbofans
summary: The 777F is the cargo version of the Boeing 777, based on the long-range 777-200LR. It can carry about 100 tonnes of freight across oceans, from fresh food to cars and medicines.
funFacts: The first 777F was delivered to Air France on 19 February 2009.
It has no passenger windows, so the outside looks like a smooth tube with only a few doors.
It can fly nearly 9,200 km fully loaded, letting airlines carry cargo between continents without stopping.
A new 777-8 Freighter based on the 777X is being developed to replace it.
spotterTips: It looks like a 777, with the same six-wheel landing gear and huge engines, but has no row of windows along the body and a large cargo door on the left side behind the wing.

melbourne.where: Visits Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) on international cargo flights, often at night or early morning.

name: Airbus BelugaXL
role: Outsize cargo aircraft for carrying aircraft parts
summary: The BelugaXL is a giant cargo plane built from an Airbus A330 with a huge bubble-shaped upper body. Airbus uses it to fly big aircraft parts, such as wings and fuselage sections, between its factories in Europe.
funFacts: It can carry two A350 wings at once, while the older BelugaST could carry only one.
Its painted eyes and smile make it look like a beluga whale, and the design was picked in a vote by Airbus employees.
The cockpit sits lower than the cargo deck so the whole nose can swing up for loading.
Its bulging cargo hold is about 1.7 m wider than the older BelugaST's.
spotterTips: Impossible to miss: a huge rounded hump above a low cockpit, like a whale's head, with A330 wings and engines. Most are painted white with a whale face on the nose.

name: Boeing Dreamlifter
role: Outsize cargo aircraft for carrying 787 parts
summary: The Dreamlifter is a Boeing 747-400 rebuilt with an enormous swollen body to carry parts of the 787 Dreamliner from factories around the world to Boeing's assembly lines. The whole tail section swings open sideways so big parts can be slid straight in.
funFacts: Its cargo hold has a volume of about 1,840 cubic metres, three times as much as a normal 747 freighter.
In November 2013 a Dreamlifter landed by mistake at the small Jabara Airport in Wichita, Kansas, instead of a nearby air force base, and had to take off from the short runway.
Its swing tail was designed with help from a Spanish company, Gamesa.
The cargo section is not pressurised, so parts travel in the cold, thin air at cruising height.
spotterTips: A 747 front end and wings with a huge, fat body behind the cockpit that rises higher than the hump. Look for the hinge line near the tail where it swings open.

name: Antonov An-124 Ruslan
crew: Up to 8 (pilots, navigator, flight engineers, radio operator and loadmasters)
passengers: 88 in the upper deck, plus up to 120 tonnes of cargo
summary: The An-124 is one of the biggest cargo aeroplanes in the world, able to carry loads like locomotives, mining trucks and even other aircraft. With the An-225 destroyed, it is now the largest cargo plane in regular commercial service.
funFacts: Its nose swings up and its tail has a ramp, so cargo can be driven straight through from front or back.
It has 24 wheels, and its landing gear can kneel down to lower the front of the plane to the ground for easier loading.
It can carry about 120 tonnes of cargo, roughly the weight of 80 family cars.
On a ferry flight with no cargo it can fly about 14,000 km.
spotterTips: A huge high-wing aircraft with four engines, a drooping wing, a single tall tail, and a long row of wheels under the belly. The nose has a bulging upper cockpit area above an upward-opening cargo door.

melbourne.where: Occasionally visits Melbourne Airport (Tullamarine) or Avalon on special heavy-lift charter flights carrying oversized cargo.

name: Antonov An-225 Mriya
summary: The An-225 Mriya was the heaviest aeroplane ever built and the one with the largest wingspan of any aircraft in service. Only one was ever finished, and it was destroyed at Hostomel Airport near Kyiv on 27 February 2022 during the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
funFacts: It was originally built to carry the Soviet Buran space shuttle on its back.
Its maximum takeoff weight was 640 tonnes, heavier than any other aeroplane ever flown.
In May 2016 it flew a huge electrical generator to Perth in Western Australia, and crowds gathered to watch it land.
It had six engines and 32 wheels to spread out its enormous weight.
spotterTips: Six engines under a very long high wing and a twin tail with two fins at the ends of the tailplane. It looked like a stretched An-124 with a different tail.
